messages.subject: [amelia] impossible values
messages.body_plain:
I'm imputing values for missing blood lipids (roughly 20% out of 3000
observations) in a cross-sectional data set. Some of the imputed values are
not possible (for example, negative triglycerides levels). I'm not sure how
to handle these imputed values. Should I just ignore then and go ahead with
the analysis? Is it possible to impose restrictions on the model (using
Amelia) to make all triglyceride values positive?
Any suggestions will be appreciated.

Leonelo E. Bautista, MD, DrPH
Assistant Professor
University of Wisconsin Medical School
Population Health Sciences

Madison, WI 53726-2397

Fax: (608)263-2820

messages.subject: [amelia] impossible values
messages.body_plain:
think about it this way.  suppose you had a fully observed dataset and
someone with evil intent was sitting at your computer with it loaded up in
an editor.  you know that, once every minute, they will change one of the
numbers in the data set, let's suppose at random.  You have no backup.
If it will take you M minutes to get to your office, how big would M have
to be before you decide not to start sprinting and instead give up the
dataset?  It depends on lots of characteristics of the dataset of course.
Same with imputation.  Tho with out-of-bounds imputation, the changes
won't generally be random, and so might be reasonable, but you never know
for sure.  the risk with imputation is that the out-of-bounds predictions
might be telling you that the model is wrong and so the in-bounds
predictions are wrong too.  If you think that might be true, then you
should definitely think about a different imputation model, perhaps with
better covariates.

Gary

messages.subject: [amelia] impossible values
messages.body_plain:
There have been a number of interesting comments on imputations that are 
out of the bounds, and since this is a very common topic, I thought I 
would add one or two more comments.  The first two are summaries of points 
already made, the third has not come up yet.

[1] Gary's statement that lots of out of bound impuations are a signal 
that the data is not linearly related, and could probably be transformed 
to make it approximately so, is very true.  This is always the first thing 
to check.  Indeed the very idea of a bound suggests that in some region of 
the data, things are not multivariate normal.

[2] Truncation/Censoring:  There are two additional methods to deal with 
these values.  First you could round all of the out-of-bounds imputations 
to the boundary value.  This is equivalent to creating a censored 
distribution from the multivariate normal dist. that Amelia has estimated. 
There is also the routine in the Gauss version to create a check routine, 
and redraw from the same multivariate normal any imputations that fail the 
check.  This is equivalent to truncating the posterior distribution.  I 
think it takes a little bit of substantive knowledge about the data to 
decide if this is valid.

[3] DO NOTHING.  This might seem odd, but in some (testable) circumstances 
I believe the best answer is to leave in the impossible values.  Let me 
explain at length, and bear with me.  The idea of multiple imputation is 
to create estimates of missing data that reflect both the best guess of 
the missing value, and also simultaneously the true uncertainty in that 
guess.  Across the different multiply imputed datasets the mean 
imputation of any missing value is the best guess.  However, there is 
varience across the imputations to reflect the uncertainy in the estimate. 
If the model (because of the covariates) has a very certain estimate, this 
distribution will be narrow.  If the imputation is quite uncertain, then 
the distribution across the m individual imputations in the m different 
datasets will be quite large.  Let us assume the best guess of a missin 
value is reasonable, and within the bounds, but still close to the 
bounds.  However, if this estimate is very uncertain, the way the 
mulitvaiate normal model will reflect this is by adding Normally dist. 
error across the imputations, centered at this estimate.  Clearly, if 
the best  estimate was within, but near the bounds, some of these 
imputations will have to fall outside the bounds so that the dist. 
reflects the uncertainty in the estimate.

Therefore, let me rephrase the initital question.  I don't think it 
matters much if some of the imputations are outside the bounds.  This may 
be necessary to capture the uncertainty.  What would be more troubling is if 
the MEAN imputation, across the m datasets is outside the bound.  This may 
happen, and is really the problem that needs to be corrected by one of the 
two ideas above.  You could test to see if this is a problem by averaging 
all the imputed datasets together, and checking if any of these average 
values are outside the bounds.

james.
